rules.title: System Integrity Protection is disabled
rules.summary: System Integrity Protection stops any software, even with your admin password, from changing macOS system files. With it off, malware can hide inside the system and survive updates.
rules.remedy: Restart into Recovery (hold the power button on Apple silicon), open Terminal from the Utilities menu, run csrutil enable, then restart.

rules.title: Gatekeeper is disabled
rules.summary: Gatekeeper blocks apps that aren't from the App Store or an identified, notarized developer. With it off, any downloaded app can run without a warning.
rules.remedy: Open Terminal and run sudo spctl --global-enable, then check System Settings › Privacy & Security allows apps from the App Store and identified developers.

rules.title: Application Firewall is disabled
rules.summary: The Application Firewall blocks incoming connections to apps you haven't allowed. With it off, any service on your Mac can be reached from the network you're on.
rules.remedy: Open System Settings › Network › Firewall and turn it on.

rules.title: Launch item downloads and runs a remote script
rules.summary: A launch item starts automatically and fetches code from the internet to run it. This is the most common way malware installs itself and updates.
rules.remedy: Show the plist in Finder. If you don't know what installed it, run launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) <path> for a LaunchAgent (or sudo launchctl bootout system <path> for a LaunchDaemon), move the file to the Trash, and restart.

rules.title: Launch item runs a program from a temp or shared folder
rules.summary: Real apps don't start programs from temporary or shared folders. Malware drops its program there because every user can write to them.
rules.remedy: Show the plist in Finder, unload it with launchctl bootout, then move the plist and the program it points to into the Trash.

rules.title: Launch item runs an inline script
rules.summary: The launch item runs a script written directly in its settings instead of a real app. Installers rarely do this; adware and malware often do.
rules.remedy: Read the command in the finding. If it isn't from software you installed on purpose, unload it with launchctl bootout and move the plist to the Trash.

rules.title: Shell startup file runs remote or hidden code
rules.summary: This line runs every time you open Terminal and downloads code from the internet, or decodes hidden code, and runs it.
rules.remedy: Open the file in a text editor (open -e <file>), delete the line, save, and open a new Terminal window.

rules.title: Shell startup file injects a library into every program
rules.summary: DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES loads extra code into every program started from your shell. Attackers use it to spy on commands and steal credentials.
rules.remedy: Open the file in a text editor, delete the DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES line, save, and open a new Terminal window.

rules.title: Reverse shell is running
rules.summary: A process is connecting a shell back to another computer. Whoever is on the other side can type commands on your Mac right now.
rules.remedy: Disconnect from the network, quit the process in Activity Monitor, then scan again to find the launch item or cron job that started it. Change your passwords from another device.

rules.title: Cryptocurrency miner is running
rules.summary: A cryptocurrency miner is running. Unless you started it, someone is using your Mac's power for their profit, and it usually arrives with other malware.
rules.remedy: Quit it in Activity Monitor, then scan again to find and remove the launch item that starts it.

rules.title: Mass network scanner is running (worm spreading)
rules.summary: A tool that scans large parts of the internet or your network is running. Worms use these to find their next victims.
rules.remedy: If you didn't start it, quit it in Activity Monitor and look for the launch item that started it.

rules.title: Cron job downloads or runs hidden code
rules.summary: A scheduled job downloads or decodes code and runs it on a timer, so malware keeps coming back.
rules.remedy: Run crontab -e in Terminal, delete the line, and save.

rules.title: Port commonly used by backdoors is listening
rules.summary: A program is listening on a port that backdoors and hacking tools use by default. Others on your network may be able to connect to it.
rules.remedy: The finding shows which program has the port open. If you don't recognize it, quit it and remove whatever starts it.

rules.title: IRC port used by botnets and worms is listening
rules.summary: Botnets and worms use IRC ports to receive commands. A listener here can mean your Mac is part of one.
rules.remedy: Quit the program shown in the finding unless you run an IRC server on purpose.

rules.title: Remote access service is on
rules.summary: Remote Login (SSH) or Screen Sharing is on. That's fine if you use it, but it lets others on your network try to log in.
rules.remedy: If you don't use it, turn off Remote Login and Screen Sharing in System Settings › General › Sharing. Otherwise ignore this finding.

rules.title: Silver Sparrow malware files
rules.summary: Silver Sparrow is a macOS malware family that checks in with its servers every hour and can download and run anything its authors send.
rules.remedy: Move the files listed to the Trash, unload the launch agents with launchctl bootout, and restart.

rules.title: EvilQuest (ThiefQuest) ransomware files
rules.summary: EvilQuest encrypts your files for ransom, steals files and records keystrokes.
rules.remedy: Disconnect from the network, unload the launch item with launchctl bootout, move the files to the Trash, and restore encrypted files from a backup.

rules.title: KeRanger ransomware files
rules.summary: KeRanger is ransomware that arrived inside a hacked Transmission installer and encrypts your documents.
rules.remedy: Move the files to the Trash, delete the infected app, and restore encrypted files from a backup.

rules.title: Keydnap backdoor files
rules.summary: Keydnap is a backdoor that steals passwords from your keychain and lets attackers control your Mac.
rules.remedy: Unload and delete the launch agent and the icloudsyncd file, then change the passwords stored in your keychain from another device.

rules.title: FruitFly backdoor files
rules.summary: FruitFly is a backdoor that can take screenshots, turn on the camera and log keystrokes.
rules.remedy: Unload the launch agent, move ~/.client and the plist to the Trash, and restart.

rules.title: Proton remote access trojan files
rules.summary: Proton is a remote access trojan spread through a hacked video player installer. It steals passwords, keychains and browser data.
rules.remedy: Delete the files and the infected app, then change your passwords from another device.

rules.title: EICAR antivirus test file (harmless, used to test the scanner)
rules.summary: This is the EICAR test file, which every antivirus treats as a threat on purpose. It is harmless and only proves the scanner works.
rules.remedy: Move it to the Trash when you're done testing.

rules.title: Launch item starts an unsigned or tampered program
rules.summary: Software that starts by itself at login or boot is almost always signed by its developer. An unsigned, ad-hoc signed or modified program here is how most macOS malware keeps itself running.
rules.remedy: Show the launch item in Finder and look up the program it starts. If you didn't install it, unload it with launchctl bootout, move the plist and the program to the Trash, and restart.

rules.title: App is unsigned or its signature is broken
rules.summary: Gatekeeper would refuse to open this app, so it runs only because Gatekeeper was bypassed. Cracked and trojanized apps look like this, and so do apps whose files changed after the developer signed them.
rules.remedy: If you didn't build it yourself or knowingly allow it, delete the app and download it again from the developer or the App Store. If an app updates itself into this state, reinstalling it fixes the signature.

rules.title: App is signed with a Developer ID but not notarized
rules.summary: Since macOS Catalina, Apple scans each Developer ID app for malware before Gatekeeper opens it without a warning, a step called notarization. This build was never notarized, so Apple never scanned it and Gatekeeper only opens it after someone clicks Open Anyway or it arrives without a download warning. Many apps from before 2020 look like this and are fine; its developer is still identified by the signature.
rules.remedy: Look for a newer version on the developer's website; current releases are almost always notarized. If the app is old and you trust its developer, ignore this finding. If you don't know where it came from, quit it and move it to the Trash.

rules.title: Atomic Stealer (AMOS) backdoor files
rules.summary: Atomic Stealer is the most widespread macOS stealer. It takes passwords, browser data and crypto wallets, and newer versions leave a backdoor that restarts itself and takes commands every minute. Assume your passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets were stolen.
rules.remedy: Disconnect from the network. Run sudo launchctl bootout system /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.finder.helper.plist, delete the plist and the hidden .helper, .agent and .mainhelper files in your home folder, and restart. From another device, change your Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: CrashStealer files
rules.summary: CrashStealer poses as Apple's crash reporter, asks for your password, copies your keychain and browser data, and starts again at every login. Assume your passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets were stolen.
rules.remedy: Run launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.crashreporter.helper.plist, delete the files listed, and restart. From another device, change your Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: ClickLock stealer and GSocket backdoor files
rules.summary: ClickLock arrives through fake 'paste this into Terminal' instructions. It steals browser data and installs a GSocket backdoor disguised as iCloud that gives attackers a remote shell. Assume your passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets were stolen.
rules.remedy: Unload both launch agents with launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) <plist>, delete the files listed, and restart. From another device, change your Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: Sapphire Sleet (North Korea) backdoor files
rules.summary: Sapphire Sleet is a North Korean group that targets crypto and finance workers with fake Zoom and Teams updates. Its backdoors run as fake Google and Apple services and steal credentials and wallets.
rules.remedy: Treat this Mac as compromised: disconnect it, back up only your documents, erase and reinstall macOS, then change every password from a clean device. Report it to your security team if this is a work Mac.

rules.title: ICMacOS (Icarus) stealer files
rules.summary: ICMacOS steals credentials and keeps remote access through a launch agent with an Apple-like name. Assume your passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets were stolen.
rules.remedy: Run launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.systemupdater.plist, delete the files listed, and restart. From another device, change your Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: Launch item pretends to be part of macOS
rules.summary: Apple's own launch items live only in /System, which nothing else can write to. A com.apple.* launch item in your Library or /Library was put there by something else, which is how several 2026 stealers hide.
rules.remedy: Show the plist in Finder and look at the program it starts. Unless you know which app installed it, unload it with launchctl bootout and move the plist and its program to the Trash.

rules.title: Stealer is collecting or uploading data right now
rules.summary: A running process is doing what macOS stealers do: zipping your data into a temporary folder and uploading it, showing a fake password prompt, or running a downloaded AppleScript.
rules.remedy: Disconnect from the network now, quit the process in Activity Monitor, and scan again to find what started it. From another device, change your Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: Stealer backdoor is running
rules.summary: A process matching a known backdoor is running: AMOS's hidden .helper or .agent loop, ClickLock's fake SystemUIServer, SHub's fake GoogleUpdate, Odyssey's bot loop or SOCKS proxy, PamStealer's fake Finder, Contagious Interview's .task payload, AmnesiaStealer's hidden browser, or the backdoor from the hijacked axios npm releases. Attackers can send it commands.
rules.remedy: Disconnect from the network, then follow the steps for the matching malware files finding. Killing the process alone isn't enough; AMOS restarts it within a second and PamStealer within 15 seconds.

rules.title: SSH key can log in to your Mac
rules.summary: Anyone holding the private half of this key can log in as you without a password whenever Remote Login is on. Attackers add their own key here to keep access even after you change your password.
rules.remedy: If you added this key yourself, ignore this finding; a new key will still show up. Otherwise delete its line from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, and turn off Remote Login in System Settings › General › Sharing if you don't use it.

rules.title: Profile controls your proxy, DNS, certificates or browser
rules.summary: This configuration profile can route your traffic through someone else's proxy or DNS, trust their certificate so they can read encrypted traffic, or force browser settings and extensions. Adware and spyware install profiles like this because they survive deleting the app.
rules.remedy: Unless your school or company installed it, remove it in System Settings › General › Device Management, then check your browser's search engine and extensions.

rules.title: Configuration profile is installed
rules.summary: Configuration profiles change system settings and are normally installed only by schools and companies. This one is listed so you know it's there.
rules.remedy: If you recognize it, ignore this finding. Otherwise remove it in System Settings › General › Device Management.

rules.title: Browser extension not from an official store
rules.summary: This extension updates from somewhere other than the Chrome Web Store, Edge Add-ons or Mozilla, or isn't signed by Mozilla. Malware installs extensions this way to read your browsing, steal sessions and swap search results, because store review can't stop it.
rules.remedy: Remove it from the browser's extensions page. If it keeps coming back, look for a configuration profile or launch item that reinstalls it (Bluehat checks both), then change passwords for sites you used while it was installed.

rules.title: Browser extension can read cookies on every site
rules.summary: With cookie access on every site, this extension could take over any account you're signed in to. Many honest extensions ask for this, but it's the permission session-stealing extensions need.
rules.remedy: Keep it only if you trust the developer and use it. Otherwise remove it, or limit it to specific sites in the browser's extension settings.

rules.title: Browser extension can debug pages or reroute traffic
rules.summary: The debugger permission lets an extension read and change everything on a page, including passwords as you type them. The proxy permission lets it send all your browsing through another server. VPN and developer tools need these; malicious extensions abuse them.
rules.remedy: Keep it only if it's a VPN or developer tool you installed on purpose. Otherwise remove it.

rules.title: Hijacked chalk and debug releases (September 2025 npm compromise)
rules.summary: On 8 September 2025 an attacker phished the maintainer of chalk, debug and 17 related packages and published versions with code that hijacks crypto wallet transactions in web pages. These packages are installed billions of times a week, so most JavaScript projects pulled one in that day.

rules.title: Code hidden off-screen in a project config file
rules.summary: A line in a config file in this project has a run of 150 or more spaces or tabs before or after code, which pushes the rest of the line far off the edge of an editor. Fake job interview projects hide malware this way in tailwind.config.js, next.config.js and similar files, which run as soon as the project is built or started.

rules.title: Config file runs decoded code
rules.summary: A config file in this project passes base64, hex or character-code data to eval or Function, which runs it as code. Normal build configs never do this; it is how malware in fake interview projects and hijacked packages hides its payload.

rules.title: Config file starts a command that reaches the internet
rules.summary: A config file in this project runs a shell command together with a download from the internet. Config files run every time the project is built or started, so this lets whoever wrote it run any code on your Mac.

rules.title: Config file runs code downloaded from the internet
rules.summary: A config file in this project turns a downloaded response into code and runs it, giving it access to require. This is the loader used by fake job interview projects: the real malware is fetched from a server each time the project starts.

rules.title: Obfuscated code in a project config file
rules.summary: A config file in this project contains code run through an obfuscator (names such as _0x4f2a1c). Build configs are written by hand and never need this; malware in fake interview projects and hijacked packages uses it to hide what it does.

rules.title: Large encoded blob in a project config file
rules.summary: A config file in this project holds a string of 1,000 or more base64 characters. Malware in project configs often carries its payload this way and decodes it at run time. Inline images and fonts start with data: and are not matched.

rules.title: npm install script downloads and runs code
rules.summary: This package.json has an install script (preinstall, install, postinstall or prepare) that downloads a file and runs it. npm runs these scripts on npm install without asking, so the download runs as you before you have looked at the project.
rules.remedy: Don't run npm install in this project. If you already did, treat the Mac as compromised: first act on Bluehat's other findings, because a worm's token monitor can erase your home folder if a token is revoked before it's removed. Then from another device rotate npm, GitHub and cloud tokens and SSH keys. Install unfamiliar projects with npm install --ignore-scripts.

rules.title: npm install script runs inline code that reaches the internet
rules.summary: This package.json has an install script that runs inline JavaScript with node -e and reaches the internet or starts commands. npm runs it on npm install without asking, so a downloaded payload runs before you have looked at the project.
rules.remedy: Don't run npm install in this project. If you already did, treat the Mac as compromised: first act on Bluehat's other findings, because a worm's token monitor can erase your home folder if a token is revoked before it's removed. Then from another device rotate npm, GitHub and cloud tokens and SSH keys. Install unfamiliar projects with npm install --ignore-scripts.

rules.title: Shai-Hulud npm worm scripts
rules.summary: The Shai-Hulud worm (September 2025) spread through hijacked npm packages. It drops these scripts to push a secret-stealing workflow into your GitHub repositories and to make your private repositories public, after stealing npm, GitHub and cloud tokens from this Mac.
rules.remedy: Delete the two scripts. From another device revoke and replace your npm and GitHub tokens, cloud keys and SSH keys, look for a public repository named Shai-Hulud and repositories ending in -migration in your GitHub account, and remove the infected package version from your projects.

rules.title: Shai-Hulud 2.0 GitHub runner installed
rules.summary: The Shai-Hulud 2.0 worm (November 2025) installs a GitHub Actions runner in the hidden .dev-env folder of your home folder and registers it as SHA1HULUD, so the attackers can run any command on this Mac through GitHub. If it finds no tokens to steal it erases your home folder instead.
rules.remedy: Stop the runner (quit any Runner.Listener process in Activity Monitor), delete the .dev-env folder in your home folder, and remove self-hosted runners named SHA1HULUD from your GitHub repositories. From another device revoke and replace your npm and GitHub tokens, cloud keys and SSH keys.

rules.title: Shai-Hulud 2.0 GitHub runner is being registered
rules.summary: A running process is registering this Mac as a GitHub Actions runner named SHA1HULUD, the backdoor of the Shai-Hulud 2.0 npm worm. Once registered, the attackers can run any command on this Mac through GitHub.
rules.remedy: Disconnect from the network, quit the process in Activity Monitor and delete the .dev-env folder in your home folder. From another device revoke and replace your npm and GitHub tokens, cloud keys and SSH keys, and remove self-hosted runners named SHA1HULUD from your GitHub repositories.

rules.title: Mini Shai-Hulud and ChainDrop token monitor files
rules.summary: The Mini Shai-Hulud and ChainDrop npm worms (May to October 2026, including TanStack, keyv and tensorlake) keep a stolen GitHub token on disk. gh-token-monitor checks it every minute, and in the tensorlake version, if GitHub rejects the token it erases your home folder.
rules.remedy: Don't revoke any GitHub token yet: while the monitor runs, revoking it from any device can erase your home folder. Back up what you can't lose. Run launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.gh-token-monitor.plist, delete the files listed and the gh-token-monitor folder, and restart. Only then, from another device, revoke and replace your GitHub and npm tokens, cloud keys and SSH keys.

rules.title: Mini Shai-Hulud or ChainDrop worm is running
rules.summary: A running process matches the Mini Shai-Hulud or ChainDrop npm worm: its gh-token-monitor script or its Bun payload. It steals GitHub, npm and cloud tokens and uses them to publish infected versions of your packages.
rules.remedy: Don't revoke any GitHub token yet: while the monitor runs, revoking it from any device can erase your home folder. Disconnect from the network, quit the process in Activity Monitor, then follow the steps for the token monitor files finding. Only after that, from another device, revoke and replace your GitHub and npm tokens, cloud keys and SSH keys.

rules.title: Files left by the nx s1ngularity stealer
rules.summary: The hijacked nx releases of August 2025 (s1ngularity) made AI coding tools on the Mac list wallets, keys and secret files into /tmp/inventory.txt, then uploaded them to a public GitHub repository named s1ngularity-repository.
rules.remedy: Open the file to check it lists your key and wallet files, then delete it. From another device revoke and replace your GitHub and npm tokens and SSH keys, move any crypto to a new wallet, and look for a repository containing s1ngularity-repository in your GitHub account.

rules.title: Shutdown trap from the nx s1ngularity stealer
rules.summary: Your shell startup file runs sudo shutdown -h 0, which the hijacked nx releases of August 2025 (s1ngularity) added to ~/.zshrc and ~/.bashrc. Every new Terminal window asks for your password and shuts the Mac down. The same malware uploaded your keys and wallet files to GitHub.
rules.remedy: Remove the sudo shutdown -h 0 line from ~/.zshrc and ~/.bashrc in a text editor (don't open a new Terminal window first). From another device revoke and replace your GitHub and npm tokens and SSH keys, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: System or kernel extension from an unlisted vendor
rules.summary: System and kernel extensions run with more power than apps: they can filter or reroute network traffic, watch every file and process, or drive hardware, and they keep running after their app quits. Spyware and adware install them for that reason. This one isn't from a vendor on Bluehat's short list of well-known ones, which doesn't make it bad: many genuine VPNs, security tools and device drivers aren't listed.
rules.remedy: If you know the app it came from, ignore this finding. Otherwise open System Settings › General › Login Items & Extensions, turn the extension off, and delete the app that installed it. For a kernel extension, run the vendor's uninstaller and restart.

rules.title: XProtect malware definitions are out of date
rules.summary: XProtect is the malware scanner built into macOS. Apple updates its definitions on its own every few weeks, and old definitions miss current stealers and backdoors. Updates usually stop when Install Security Responses and system files is turned off, or when the Mac can't reach Apple's servers.
rules.remedy: Open System Settings › General › Software Update, click the info button next to Automatic Updates, and turn on Install Security Responses and system files. Stay online and restart; macOS updates XProtect on its own. If it still shows a day later, install any waiting macOS update.

rules.title: SHub (Reaper) stealer backdoor files
rules.summary: SHub steals passwords, browser data, the Keychain, Telegram sessions and crypto wallets, and its Reaper version swaps wallet apps for tampered copies. It hides a backdoor in a fake GoogleUpdate.app that a launch agent named like Google's real updater (com.google.keystone.agent.plist) runs every minute to take commands. Assume your passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets were stolen.
rules.remedy: Run launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.google.keystone.agent.plist and delete that plist only if it starts GoogleUpdate.app (Google's real updater uses the same name). Delete the files listed, reinstall your wallet apps from their developers, and restart. From another device, change your Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: Launch item starts SHub's fake Google updater
rules.summary: This launch item starts GoogleUpdate.app, the backdoor of the SHub (Reaper) stealer, which asks its server for commands every minute. Google's updaters on macOS are GoogleSoftwareUpdateAgent.app and GoogleUpdater.app; Google ships no GoogleUpdate.app. SHub names its launch agent com.google.keystone.agent.plist, the same as Google's real one, so only the program it starts tells them apart.
rules.remedy: Run launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) <plist> for the plist in the finding, move it and ~/Library/Application Support/Google/GoogleUpdate.app to the Trash, and restart. Chrome sets up its real updater again on its own. From another device, change your Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: Odyssey stealer backdoor files
rules.summary: Odyssey, the successor of Poseidon, steals passwords, browser data, the Keychain and crypto wallets and can replace Ledger Live with a fake copy. It installs a backdoor that runs from a randomly named LaunchDaemon (com.<random>.plist) and keeps its bot ID in the hidden .botid file in your home folder. Assume your passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets were stolen.
rules.remedy: Disconnect from the network. Find the com.<random>.plist in /Library/LaunchDaemons you don't recognize, run sudo launchctl bootout system <plist> and delete it. Delete the files listed, delete Ledger Live and download it again from ledger.com, and restart. From another device, change your Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: Banshee stealer files
rules.summary: Banshee shows a fake system settings password prompt, checks the password you type, then copies the Keychain, browser passwords and cookies, Notes and crypto wallets and uploads them. It leaves the password-entered file in your home folder. It doesn't start again after a restart, but what it took is already gone. Assume your passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets were stolen.
rules.remedy: Delete the files listed and the app or installer that started it, then restart. From another device, change your Mac login, Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: Poseidon stealer working folder
rules.summary: Poseidon, spread through fake Arc browser ads and fake AGOV emails, copies the Keychain, browser passwords and cookies, Notes, VPN settings and crypto wallets into /tmp/xuyna, zips them and uploads them. It doesn't start again after a restart, but what it took is already gone. Assume your passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets were stolen.
rules.remedy: Delete /tmp/xuyna and /tmp/out.zip, delete the app that started it, and restart. From another device, change your Mac login, Apple Account, email and banking passwords, sign out of other sessions, and move any crypto to a new wallet.

rules.title: Browser extension hijacked in the Cyberhaven campaign (December 2024)
rules.summary: In 2024 attackers phished the developers of Cyberhaven and dozens of other Chrome extensions, or bought their extensions, and pushed updates that steal cookies, session tokens and Facebook business accounts. This extension shipped that code and has had no clean release since, or was removed from the Chrome Web Store. Removal from the store doesn't uninstall it.
rules.remedy: Remove it from the browser's extensions page. Then sign out of all sessions and change the passwords of sites you used while it was installed, Facebook and Meta Business first, and turn on two-factor authentication.

rules.title: Browser extension once hijacked in the Cyberhaven campaign, fixed since
rules.summary: Attackers took over this extension in the 2024 Cyberhaven campaign and shipped a release that stole cookies and session tokens; its developer has published a clean update since. Bluehat can't see which version you have, so it reports every copy.
rules.remedy: Turn on Developer mode on the extensions page and check the version is newer than the hijacked one: Cyberhaven 24.10.4, GraphQL Network Inspector 2.22.6, Internxt VPN 1.1.1, Castorus 4.40, TinaMind 2.13.0, Primus 3.18.0, Tackker 1.3, Visual Effects for Google Meet 3.1.3, YesCaptcha 1.1.61, Proxy SwitchyOmega (V3) 3.0.2. Then ignore this finding. If you had the hijacked version, sign out of all sessions and change the passwords of sites you used then.

rules.title: Trojanized browser extension that strips site security (GitLab, February 2025)
rules.summary: GitLab found 16 Chrome extensions (ad blockers, emoji keyboards, screen capture, KProxy and others, 3.2 million users) that a threat actor took over and changed to remove the Content Security Policy of the sites you visit and inject its own code, for ad fraud and with a risk of leaking what you see and type. Google took them down, but that doesn't uninstall them.
rules.remedy: Remove it from the browser's extensions page, then change the passwords of sites you signed in to while it was installed and sign out of their other sessions.

rules.title: Browser extension from the RedDirection hijacking campaign (July 2025)
rules.summary: Koi Security found 18 Chrome and Edge extensions (Geco color picker, weather, VPN unblockers, volume boosters and others, 2.3 million users) that turned malicious through an update: they report every site you visit to their server and can redirect you to any page, such as a fake login or update.
rules.remedy: Remove it from the browser's extensions page, clear the browser's cookies and site data, and change the passwords of sites you signed in to while it was installed.

rules.title: Browser extension from the ShadyPanda spyware campaign (December 2025)
rules.summary: Koi Security tied these Chrome and Edge extensions (Clean Master, WeTab, wallpaper and new tab pages, 4.3 million users) to one actor that, through updates, ran code downloaded from its servers every hour, sent every page you visit, search and click to servers in China, and hijacked searches and affiliate links.
rules.remedy: Remove it from the browser's extensions page, clear the browser's cookies and site data, and change the passwords of sites you signed in to while it was installed.

rules.title: Tampered Claude Code extension from Cursor's marketplace (October 2026)
rules.summary: On October 29, 2026 tampered copies of the Claude Code extension, versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, were published to Cursor's extension marketplace. They add an attacker's SSH key and open a hidden tunnel so the attacker can log in to this Mac. They also send details about the Mac to the attacker. Anthropic's own downloads were not affected.

rules.summary: Some HTTP/2 implementations are vulnerable to a reset flood, potentially leading to a denial of service. The attacker opens a number of streams and sends an invalid request over each stream that should solicit a stream of RST_STREAM frames from the peer. Depending on how the peer queues the RST_STREAM frames, this can consume excess memory, CPU, or both.
rules.remedy: Upgrade Node.js to 8.16.1, 10.16.3, 12.8.1 or a later release on the same line, in each listed install. For affected versions with no listed fix, upgrade to a later supported Node.js release.

rules.summary: Some HTTP/2 implementations are vulnerable to a settings flood, potentially leading to a denial of service. The attacker sends a stream of SETTINGS frames to the peer. Since the RFC requires that the peer reply with one acknowledgement per SETTINGS frame, an empty SETTINGS frame is almost equivalent in behavior to a ping. Depending on how efficiently this data is queued, this can consume excess CPU, memory, or both.
rules.remedy: Upgrade Node.js to 8.16.1, 10.16.3, 12.8.1 or a later release on the same line, in each listed install. For affected versions with no listed fix, upgrade to a later supported Node.js release.

rules.summary: Some HTTP/2 implementations are vulnerable to unconstrained interal data buffering, potentially leading to a denial of service. The attacker opens the HTTP/2 window so the peer can send without constraint; however, they leave the TCP window closed so the peer cannot actually write (many of) the bytes on the wire. The attacker then sends a stream of requests for a large response object. Depending on how the servers queue the responses, this can consume excess memory, CPU, or both.
rules.remedy: Upgrade Node.js to 8.16.1, 10.16.3, 12.8.1 or a later release on the same line, in each listed install. For affected versions with no listed fix, upgrade to a later supported Node.js release.

The peer spends time processing each frame disproportionate to attack bandwidth. This can consume excess CPU.
rules.remedy: Upgrade Node.js to 8.16.1, 10.16.3, 12.8.1 or a later release on the same line, in each listed install. For affected versions with no listed fix, upgrade to a later supported Node.js release.

rules.title: PHP: Information Leak of Memory in getimagesize (CVE-2025-14177)

This may lead to information disclosure of sensitive heap data and affect the confidentiality of the target server.
rules.remedy: Upgrade PHP to 8.1.34, 8.2.30, 8.3.29, 8.4.16 or a later release on the same line, in each listed install. For affected versions with no listed fix, upgrade to a later supported PHP release.

rules.summary: There is a LOW severity vulnerability affecting CPython, specifically the 'http.cookies' standard library module. rules.title: Python: Infinite loop when iterating over zip archive entry names from zipfile.Path (CVE-2024-8088)
rules.summary: There is a HIGH severity vulnerability affecting the CPython "zipfile" module affecting "zipfile.Path". Note that the more common API "zipfile.ZipFile" class is unaffected. When iterating over names of entries in a zip archive (for example, methods of "zipfile.Path" like "namelist()", "iterdir()", etc) the process can be put into an infinite loop with a maliciously crafted zip archive. This defect applies when reading only metadata or extracting the contents of the zip archive. Programs that are not handling user-controlled zip archives are not affected.
rules.remedy: Upgrade Python to 3.8.20, 3.9.20, 3.10.15, 3.11.10, 3.12.6 or a later release on the same line, in each listed install.

rules.title: Python: Virtual environment (venv) activation scripts don't quote paths (CVE-2024-9287)
rules.summary: A vulnerability has been found in the CPython `venv` module and CLI where path names provided when creating a virtual environment were not quoted properly, allowing the creator to inject commands into virtual environment "activation" scripts (ie "source venv/bin/activate"). Virtual environments which are not created by an attacker or which aren't activated before being used (ie "./venv/bin/python") are not affected.

rules.summary: There is a defect in the CPython “tarfile” module affecting the “TarFile” extraction and entry enumeration APIs. rules.title: Python: The expat and elementtree parsers use insufficient entropy for XML hash-flooding protection (CVE-2026-7210)

The extraction fallback validated the symlink at it's archived location but recreated it at the hardlink's shallower path, letting a relative target the filter judged contained escape the destination directory. This allowed a malicious tar archive to create a symlink pointing outside the destination, enabling out-of-destination file reads or writes. This was an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-4330.

rules.title: Ruby: Ruby before 2.4.3 allows Net::FTP command injection. (CVE-2017-17405)
rules.summary: Ruby before 2.4.3 allows Net::FTP command injection. Net::FTP#get, getbinaryfile, gettextfile, put, putbinaryfile, and puttextfile use Kernel#open to open a local file. If the localfile argument starts with the "|" pipe character, the command following the pipe character is executed. The default value of localfile is File.basename(remotefile), so malicious FTP servers could cause arbitrary command execution.

rules.title: Ruby: An issue was discovered in Ruby 4 before 4.0.5. (CVE-2026-46727)
rules.summary: An issue was discovered in Ruby 4 before 4.0.5. A race condition leading to a use-after-free in the pthread-based getaddrinfo timeout handler (rb_getaddrinfo in ext/socket/raddrinfo.c) allows a remote attacker who can delay DNS responses near the user-specified timeout to crash a Ruby process that calls Addrinfo.getaddrinfo(..., timeout:) or Socket.tcp(..., resolv_timeout:). Memory-corruption-based exploitation is theoretically possible. The attack could, for example, be carried out through a crafted authoritative DNS server or recursive resolver.
rules.remedy: Upgrade Ruby to 4.0.5 or a later release on the same line, in each listed install.
